paragraphs.text: I wanted to carry my reflections on the cross through to the end. I do not claim to have mastered their meaning; I only mean to set out for the faithful as much as can be grasped. Words are not enough to explain the divine oracles. What is said is measured by human capacity, and not because that capacity is enough to comprehend them, but because God supplies it: not as much as the giver can give, but as much as the receiver can hold. A mother could give solid bread to the infant she is nursing, but the child is not strong enough to take it. In the same way it is not impossible for God to give us the greater wisdom that is beyond this world, but we are unable to receive it, for we live in a mortal body. So God has said nothing to us with the perfection that befits him. He has measured what he says to our weakness. That is why the Savior said, "I have many things to say, but you cannot bear them now." And elsewhere the Savior said to Nicodemus, "If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe [?], how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?" Let us speak, then, as far as human capacity reaches, with God supplying it. But today has interrupted our discourse, though we wanted to take our reflections in order. It was interrupted by the reading of the Gospel, but that will be spoken of at its proper time. Let us call to mind what happened on this very day. Today, on this fifth day of the week, in the evening before his Passion, Christ washed the disciples' feet, kept the Passover that the Law had prefigured, and handed down the saving mystery of his Passion. So, to tell the truth, the discourse of truth is not really interrupted at all. That narrative is about the cross too, and so our rule is kept. Let us come, then, to the sequence of events, cutting it short [?] so as to give your Christ-loving souls a few tastes. Let us give a brief and clear account of how one ought to understand the contemplation of our holy and mystical traditions. The Savior says to the disciples, "You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man is handed over to be crucified." The Savior often foretold this to his disciples. He was showing that he knew and did not flee, and foresaw it and did not refuse it. He was also preparing the apostles' souls in advance, so that, being forewarned, they might escape confusion. What has been thought over beforehand does not bring the turmoil of a sudden shock. David foretold this as well: "I was prepared and was not troubled." The same thing happens with thunder. The lightning comes first and teaches the mind to expect the thunder, so that the expectation may relieve the greater fear. So too the Savior, so that [the apostles might] not [be overwhelmed] all at once by the Passion [?], reproached them and said after the resurrection, "These are my words that I spoke to you, that the Son of Man must suffer many things." He reproached them because they had not achieved the purpose for which the Savior had foretold it. "I told you beforehand," he means, "so that you would not stumble, and still your confusion got the better of you." "You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man is about to be handed over to be crucified." Nowhere will you find the Savior mentioning his Passion without bringing in the human person, speaking as though one were talking about another. He did not say, "I am handed over," but "The Son of Man is about to be handed over to be crucified." Nowhere will you find the Savior handed over; it is "the Son of Man" who is handed over. Everywhere he speaks as one about another. But when it concerns his divinity, he speaks plainly: "I and the Father are one." He does not say, "I and the Father who sent me," but "I and the Father are one," and "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." "You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man is handed over to be crucified." And how carefully does John put it? So that no one would think that what happened at that time was forced on him, see how he guards against it: "Knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own, he loved them to the end." That is, he showed a perfect love. "And when supper was over, he rose, laid aside his garments, girded himself with the towel, poured water into the basin and began to wash the disciples' feet." Let the heretics be ashamed. When they hear the Savior saying, "I do the will of my Father," they immediately say, "You see that he is subject to the Father like a slave and obeys him." At that hour there was an awesome thing to see. Why did he who wraps himself in light as in a garment rise, lay aside his garment and gird himself with a towel? Then one could see Paul's words come true, that "being in the form of God, he took the form of a slave." He who wraps the heaven in clouds girded himself with a towel. He who poured out the waters into rivers and springs and seas poured water into a basin. Picture the disciple seated and the Master bending down and looking at the knee, he to whom every knee bends, in heaven, on earth and under the earth. The Savior's humility put out all pride. That gentleness put out all arrogance.

When I see the Savior washing the disciples' feet, I repeat what Isaiah says about our pride: "Why are earth and ashes proud?" Picture the Master stooping to his servants' feet and washing them. How can this be spoken of, or how can it be passed over in silence? Words will not be enough, and silence accuses us of ingratitude. What shall we do, then, when we cannot even speak? "He began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel." He left out no part of the service. He did not let others pour in the water while he did the washing, nor did he wash while others dried. Here he seems to be introducing his disciples to some strange mystery. "Having loved his own disciples, he loved them to the end," says John. "And when supper was over, the devil having already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him, he rose and laid aside his garments." John did not say this idly. He wanted to show that even though the traitor was planning the betrayal, the Savior did not hesitate to wash the traitor's own feet. He knew his treachery, and he washed him. What then? Is there partiality with God? By no means. Partiality always arises between wrongdoers and those they wrong. When the one who is wronged honors the wrongdoer, that is not partiality but humility. But when the one who is wronged [?] secretly does evil while putting on a show of kindness, that is hypocrisy. Take the proof from the event itself. Judas, who betrayed the Master, knew that what he was doing was impious, for he offered a kiss to the one he was plotting against. But the Savior, though wronged, honored the one who wronged him. That was not injustice but humility in its highest degree, praised by God and admired by men. Do you want to see a show of friendship? Look at Joab, David's commander-in-chief. He took aside Abner, another commander, spoke friendly words to him and secretly drove his sword into his side. He called him brother and killed him as an enemy. That is why hypocrisy is evil. But when the one who is wronged does good to the wrongdoer, the deed deserves praise. Jacob was afraid of his own brother Esau and begged God, "Deliver me from the hand of my brother, or he will come and kill me." Yet when he saw him, he honored him and said, "I have seen your face as one sees the face of God." He saw him as an enemy and a murderer, but since God knew that Jacob said this not to lay a trap but to escape one, God forgave him. So if anyone speaks friendly words not to deceive but to escape deceit, God is not angry, for he himself teaches this: "A humble word turns away wrath." So, the devil having already put it into Judas's heart to betray the Savior, the Savior wanted to conquer ingratitude with love for mankind and to undo arrogance with gentleness, and he washed his feet. I do not marvel so much at the Master doing what was natural to him (gentleness was his work) as at that man so full of deceit. With what heart did he hold out his feet? How could he watch the Master's holy hands moving over his feet? How was he not paralyzed? How did he not shudder? Yet the forbearing nature is patient. It seems, too, that he washed him first. Why? If he had not washed the traitor's feet, and had passed him over while washing the others, that too would have been unworthy of the Master, and Judas would have had a plausible excuse: "He shut me out himself. He drove me away himself. He washed everyone's feet but condemned me. How could I bring myself to stay with him?" God saw a crushed heart, and he did not want to crush what was already crushing itself. This was the meaning of "A bruised reed you shall not break." So he washed the disciples' feet. He came last to Peter. While the Savior was washing the others, Peter thought about the Master's dignity and the meanness of men, the lowliness of men and the glory of the one who is glorified, and he made up his mind not to allow it. The Savior came to him, and Peter said, "Lord, are you washing my feet?" You are the one who raises the dead and cleanses lepers (for that "you" carries great force). You are the one I bore witness to: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." If I had said it out of ignorance, it might have been only a human guess. But since you set your seal on my words when you said, "My Father in heaven revealed it to you," will you stoop to wash a servant's feet with the Master's hands? "You shall never wash my feet." What did the Savior do then? He swept his objection aside. "What I am doing you do not know now," he says, "but afterward you will understand." That is, you do not know my purpose in doing this. Peter would not accept it, and on hearing this he said, "You shall never wash my feet." He showed a soul harder than adamant. But the Savior applied his own fire and made the adamantine soul softer than wax. "So then," he says, "you stubborn and contentious man, give up your resistance. Unless I wash your feet, you have no part with me." And the stubborn, contentious man says, "Lord, not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well." He had held back the principal and repaid it with interest. The Christian character is not rigid. A Christian ought not to have a contentious [?] character. He ought not to be versatile in scheming, but versatile [?] in virtue. This is how he ought to be: cheerful in a time for cheer and somber in a time of grief, as Paul says, "Rejoice with those who rejoice," fast with those who fast, "weep with those who weep." This is what Paul means when he says, "Whether you eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God." So Peter's stubbornness did him no good, for it was overcome, just as another man's was. When Christ came to be baptized by John, the Baptist said to him, "Lord, I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?" The Savior said to him, "Let it be so now." Do not be contentious, do not resist, for this is God's purpose. Do not reveal my dignity before its time. Let me fulfill what is appointed and show truly that I have taken on a man, so that through the true man I may be revealed as God. He said only, "Let it be so now," and at once the evangelist adds, "Then he allowed him to be baptized." He contended as a devout man and obeyed as one who loved God. Jeremiah too contended with God: "O sovereign Lord, you know that I am too young." "And the Lord said to me, 'Do not say, I am too young, for you shall go to all to whom I send you.'" Firmness overcame stubbornness. Moses too was stubborn when he said, "Appoint someone else, for I am weak of voice and slow of tongue." But God did not give way.

But let us return to our subject. The Savior says, "Unless I wash your feet, you have no part with me." From this we should learn that God is the portion of the faithful, and the faithful are the portion of God. For example, the whole world belongs to God, but God knows the faithful. "I created the whole world," he says, "but nothing matters to me except the portion of the faithful." That is why the faithful cried out, as David did, "The Lord is my portion in the land of the living," and again, "The Lord is the portion of my inheritance." And Mary sat at the Master's feet and listened to his teaching, and the Savior said, "Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken from her." Do you see that God is the portion of the faithful? Next we must show where the faithful are said to be God's portion. Moses says, "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he fixed the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God, and the Lord's portion became his people Jacob." The whole world was his, but only Jacob was called his people. So too the prophet Amos says, "I looked, and behold, the Lord called for judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep and devoured the Lord's portion," meaning the people. "And I said, 'Stop, O Lord, spare Jacob, for he is very small,'" that is, do not destroy us. All this has been said because the Savior said, "Unless I wash you, you have no part with me." So God is the portion of the faithful, and the faithful are the portion of God. Peter says, "Lord, do not wash only my feet, but my hands and my head as well." Peter thought that this washing was the forgiveness of sins, and he wanted to receive forgiveness over his whole body. But it was not the forgiveness of sins. It was a lesson in reverence. Then the Savior says, "One who has bathed needs only to wash his feet. You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you." That is how these things stand. When he had washed their feet and dried them, he took his garments and reclined at table. He had kept the form of a slave, and now he reclines as Master and says with authority, "Do you not know what I have done to you?" That is, have you not understood? "Do you not call me Lord and Teacher? And you are right, for so I am." Here he reveals his authority. He has put off the form of the slave and brings forward the form of God. "Do you not call me Lord and Teacher? If I, then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another's feet? For I have given you an example" (I see that it was a lesson in reverence) "so that you also should do to one another as I have done to you."

After these things had happened, his disciples came to him and said, "Lord, where do you want us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?" See God's foreknowledge. He says, "Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him wherever he goes, and say to the master of whatever house he enters, 'My time is near; I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.' And he will show you an upper room, furnished." He does two things at once. He equips the apostles to ask the master of the house, and so that they would not think he did not know the place, he tells them, "He will show you a large upper room, furnished." If you can foretell the place, why do you tell the disciples to ask about it? Have we learned the answer before we asked? "Yes," he says, "and it is fitting for me to foretell as God and for you to ask as men." Christ never hands down the mystery in low places, but on the mountain or in an upper room, for nothing about Christ is below ground. That is why the apostles were gathered in an upper room when they received the descent of the Holy Spirit. Then, it says, he sent two of the disciples to prepare the Passover. Who were they? Peter and John. Why, of all the twelve, did he send Peter and John? Peter was the one who confessed, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." John was to proclaim, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." He sends the foundation of the faith and the son of thunder, so that on the foundation he might fix the mystery of godliness, and through the son of thunder flash forth the commandments of righteousness. Again, why does he send Peter and John? To show that the gift has been extended to both chaste marriage and virginity, and that those who live rightly in chaste marriage and those who live rightly in virginity alike become partakers of the Passover. He sends virginity and chaste marriage to prepare the Passover for him, just as on the mountain he had Moses and Elijah stand beside him, one shining with chaste marriage and the other with virginity, so that chaste marriage and virginity might be seen standing beside Christ. "I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you." No one is forcing or compelling him. The Passion is not against his will; his resolve is freely chosen. If the Master, while bestowing his benefits, said, "I have eagerly desired," what shall we say? You anticipate our words, Master. You get ahead of our sins and shine on us first with your benefits. It is we who ought to say, "We long to see the Passover," and you say it first? Does a spring ever long for the thirsty, or do the thirsty long for the spring? Does a table long for the hungry, or do the hungry long for the table? It is for us to say David's words: "As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God." But since the Savior's mystery lies before us, the glorious Passion itself, the very handing down of the Passion, the sermon must give way to the occasion, so that we who thirst may enjoy it, the faithful may be strengthened, those about to be enlightened may receive the pledge, and the faithful may be on their guard. Do not use the gift as an excuse to break off the course of the fast. Someone completing a long journey will rest to look after his body, whether at inns or in other places, but he does not give up the journey. He rests to refresh his body, but he does not abandon the goal of his journey. In the same way the Savior has given us the enjoyment of his good things, not so that we may indulge ourselves, but so that we may care for flesh and soul. So do not use the mysteries as an excuse to bring in what does not belong. Do not think, because you receive communion, that grace is sister to drunkenness. Let these things be observed not only by the faithful but also by the catechumens. Before you receive the gift, show that you value it as it deserves. What need is there for words? Examine your conscience. With what confidence does someone who has cheated on the fast come forward? You will indeed come forward tomorrow, and even if no one accuses you, your conscience will. Have you ever seen anyone carry his accuser around with him? Rather, make your conscience your advocate. This present day, that is, this holy mystery, does not want [?] the course of the fast, nor the mystery of holy Pascha. But since in this one the Passion is handed down, and in that one the resurrection is revealed, let us become partakers [of the Passion] and sharers in the resurrection. Today let us share in the Passion, and then in the resurrection. Today, as we share in it, let us give ourselves not to luxury but to tears, for after the resurrection there is no more grief. The Master is still in his Passion, and you are indulging yourself? Do you not know how many people, often even among the great, have been censured and have suffered punishment for feasting during royal mourning? And you, seeing the Master's Passion still shining on the cross, before you have even heard the word of the resurrection, have seized the joy of the resurrection in advance and given yourself over to luxury? I say this not because we must mourn the Savior himself, as though he had suffered things worth mourning, but because we must show our own gratitude, so that, having shared in his Passion, we may share in his resurrection. For to him, the Lord, belong glory, honor and worship, together with the Father and the all-holy and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
